$comment: Architecture walkthrough of the Olber escrow wallet (author's own company). Patterns only; no schema, endpoint or vendor specifics.

card.job: Clients post orders and fund them; workers bid, do the job, and get paid out. Both talk to the same backend with different roles.
card.guards: The app never computes money. It displays balances the ledger reports.
card.tradeoff: More round-trips than an optimistic client, in exchange for one source of truth.

card.job: Two small Node services: one for auth, identity verification and orders; one for payments and payouts. Both are thin — business rules live in database functions so that the mobile apps and the admin tools cannot disagree.
card.guards: Duplicate side effects: every money-moving call takes an idempotency key.
card.tradeoff: Logic in the database is harder to unit-test than in application code — hence 115 pgTAP files.

card.job: System of record. Row-level security policies decide who can read and write each row, so an authorisation bug in one client cannot expose another user's data.
card.guards: Marketplace-wide data exposure through a mis-scoped query.
card.tradeoff: RLS policies are easy to get subtly wrong. They were audited as a unit (37 findings) and remediated with tested migrations.

card.job: Every movement of money is an immutable entry: deposit, hold, release, commission, payout, reversal. Balances are sums over entries, never stored counters.
card.guards: Silent balance drift. An append-only table cannot lose history; a mistaken entry is corrected by a compensating entry, visibly.
card.tradeoff: Reads are heavier than a balance column. A materialised view carries the hot path.

card.job: Once a day, checks that deposits minus holds, releases, commissions and payouts equals the aggregator's reported balance — to the cent — and alerts on any delta.
card.guards: The class of bug that is invisible for months and then very expensive.
card.tradeoff: It found a real drift once. The fix was audited compensating entries, not editing history.

card.job: Side effects that must happen after a transaction commits (payout instruction, push notification) are written to an outbox table in the same transaction and delivered by a worker.
card.guards: The half-done state where the database committed but the external call never happened, or vice versa.
card.tradeoff: Delivery is at-least-once, so every consumer must be idempotent.

card.job: Charges cards and executes payouts. Reports events back through webhooks.
card.guards: Forged or replayed webhooks: each one is HMAC-verified and de-duplicated by event id before it can touch the ledger.
card.tradeoff: Card data is stored only in the encrypted form the aggregator's flow requires; nothing sensitive is logged.

edges.label: HTTPS
edges.flow: Authenticated requests with an idempotency key on anything that moves money
Calls to database functions under the caller's role; RLS applies

edges.label: append
edges.flow: Ledger entries written inside the same transaction as the order state change

edges.label: commit
edges.flow: Outbox rows become visible to the worker only after commit

edges.label: payout
edges.flow: Payout instruction, retried with backoff until acknowledged

edges.label: webhook
edges.flow: Signed events: charge succeeded, payout settled, chargeback
Nightly sum over all entries per wallet
Aggregator-side balance report for the same period

tour.text: A client funds an order from the app. The app sends the amount and an idempotency key; it does not touch balances.
The payments service validates the request and calls one database function. Retrying the same key returns the same result.
Inside a single transaction: the order moves to funded, a hold entry lands in the ledger, and an outbox row is written.
The ledger now has a deposit and a hold. The client's available balance is a sum, so it is already correct.
After commit, the worker picks up the outbox row and notifies the worker who bid. If the push fails, it retries; if it is delivered twice, the consumer ignores the duplicate.
When the job is accepted, a payout instruction goes to the aggregator. Its webhook comes back signed; the signature is checked before anything is written.
That night the reconciler sums every entry and compares it with the aggregator's report. Zero delta, or a page.
